config.title: Add Two Numbers

intro.title: Add Two Numbers
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple JavaScript function that adds two numbers together and returns the result. You will learn the core programming concept of function definition and how to use parameters and the return statement. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, arithmetic operators, and variable handling. This exercise will help you understand how to structure basic operations in code, a fundamental skill for all algorithmic lesson-solving.
intro.usecase: The Add Two Numbers pattern is fundamental to countless real-world applications where numerical calculations are required. In e-commerce platforms, this logic calculates total prices by adding product costs and shipping fees during checkout. Financial dashboards use it to sum revenue streams or combine investment returns across multiple accounts. Even in simple calculator apps or budgeting tools, this basic addition operation forms the core functionality that users rely on daily.

objectives: Implement a function that takes two numbers as parameters and returns their sum
Apply arithmetic operators to perform addition within a JavaScript function
Construct a complete program that prompts for user input, processes the addition, and displays the result
Configure function parameters to accept numeric values for mathematical operations
Manipulate variables to store input values and calculation results
Initialize and use variables to hold intermediate values during the addition process
Integrate user input collection with calculation logic in a single workflow

content.body: Let's solve a classic coding challenge: finding two numbers in an array that add up to a specific target. This is a fundamental pattern you'll use often. We'll start simple and build up to an efficient solution.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Identify when to use a hashmap for pair-finding lessons
2. Implement a single-pass solution using a lookup structure
3. Explain why checking before adding prevents duplicate work
4. Return indices of matching pairs correctly
5. Apply this pattern to similar array lessons
content.title: What you'll learn
One more
content.successMessage: Great! You checked pairs until you found 3 and 9 (or 5 and 7, etc.).

content.body: What you just did was brute force: you picked each element from the start and added it with others until you found the pair. That works for small arrays.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10,000 numbers, checking every pair is too slow. We need a better method. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of re-scanning the array for each number, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to remember values we've encountered. This lets us check in one step whether we've seen the number we need.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use a single pass and a lookup structure. For each number, we calculate what we need (target - current), check if we've seen it before, and either return the pair or add the current number to our notebook.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [2,7,11,15], target 9:
1. Check 2 → need 7? Not seen. Add 2 to notebook.
2. Check 7 → need 2? Yes, seen at index 0. Return [0,1].

Key decisions:
- Store the number as key, index as value
- Check BEFORE adding to avoid using same element twice

content.body:
1. Create an empty lookup object
2. Loop through each number in the array
3. For each number, calculate: needed = target - current
4. Check if needed exists in lookup
   - If yes: return [lookup[needed], current index]
   - If no: add current number to lookup with its index
5. If loop ends without finding pair, return empty array
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function skeleton
steps.instruction: Start by creating a function called twoSum that takes nums array and target number as parameters. Return an empty array for now.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure you have both parameters: nums and target.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function named twoSum that takes nums and target.

steps.title: Initialize the lookup structure
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create an empty object called seen. This will store numbers we've encountered as keys and their indices as values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! Make sure you're declaring a const variable named seen.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need an empty object to store numbers we've seen.

steps.title: Loop through the array
steps.instruction: Add a for loop to iterate through nums. Inside, calculate the needed number: target - current number.
steps.hint: for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { const needed = target - nums[i]; }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're calculating needed = target - nums[i] inside the loop.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to loop through all numbers and calculate what number we need to find.

steps.title: Check and add to lookup
steps.instruction: Inside the loop: check if needed exists in seen. If yes, return [seen[needed], i]. If no, add current number to seen with its index. After the loop, return [].
steps.hint: if (needed in seen) return [seen[needed], i]; else seen[nums[i]] = i;
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Make sure you're checking if needed is in seen BEFORE adding current number.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: check first, then add. This prevents using the same element twice.

content.body:
Great work! You've learned the hashmap approach for finding pairs. Remember:
1. Store numbers as keys, indices as values in your lookup
2. Always check if you've seen the needed number BEFORE adding the current one
3. This single-pass solution is O(n) time and O(n) space

This 'notebook' pattern works for many lessons where you need to remember what you've seen!
